Night break on ward 4. It's quiet. Jonas, his hand now healed, and Mara are drinking tea and talking about why they chose this job.
Jonas, why did you actually become a nurse?
Honestly? Because I spent a year in hospital when I was a teenager. I had a bad bike accident.
A whole year? I didn't know.
Yes. And I saw that nurses are much more important than you'd think. The doctors came for five minutes a day. The nurses were always there.
That's true. I think patients often tell us more than they tell the doctors.
Exactly. And you? Why did you come to Germany?
Because in Sibiu I earned almost nothing. And because I wanted to see something new. But my mum thinks I'm only staying for a year.
And? Are you only staying for a year?
I don't know. I miss my family, that's why I call every day. But I'm glad I'm here. I've found friends.
I hope you stay. Clara says she wants you as her maid of honour at the wedding!
Me? Really? But we've only known each other for two months!
She says a woman who bandages her fiancé's hand at one in the morning is the perfect maid of honour.
“dass” (that) and “das” (this / article) are pronounced the same: “das”. The difference is only in writing: “dass” with ss links two clauses.
In the subordinate clause, the voice rises a little before the final verb, which is stressed: “…weil ich in Berlin ARBEITE.”
1. The subordinate clause: verb at the end
Until now, the conjugated verb sat in position 2. In the SUBORDINATE clause (after weil, dass, wenn, ob…), the conjugated verb goes to the END. You ALWAYS put a comma between the two clauses.
Imagine that “weil” and “dass” are magnets that pull the verb to the end of the clause.
2. Separable verbs, modals and Perfekt in the subordinate clause
…weil ich jeden Tag anrufe. (the verb sticks back together!)
…weil ich etwas Neues sehen will. (the modal goes last)
…weil ich nichts verdient habe. (the auxiliary goes last)
The order at the end: the infinitive / participle, then the conjugated verb: “…dass er nicht kommen kann”, “…weil ich lange geschlafen habe”.
Three ways to express cause and effect, with three different word orders:
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
normal word order (denn doesn't take up a position)
Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin krank.
deshalb in position 1, the verb in position 2
Ich bin krank, deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.

As an answer to “Warum?” you use “Weil…” on its own: “Warum lernst du Deutsch? — Weil ich in Berlin lebe.” In fast speech, many Germans put the verb in position 2 after “weil” too, but in writing and in the exam: verb at the end!
“dass” introduces what you think, know, hope or feel:
Ich glaube, dass er recht hat.
Ich weiß, dass du müde bist.
Ich bin froh, dass du da bist.
Es ist schön, dass ihr kommt.
After “glauben” and “denken”, you can leave out “dass”, but then the word order is normal: “Ich glaube, er hat recht.” (just like English “I think he's right”).
“wissen” is irregular: ich weiß, du weißt, er weiß (no -t with er!), wir wissen.

It was a cold Saturday in February. Ludwig still had the cast on, so Ola and Kuba took Fritz to the Mauerpark at lunchtime. They were very proud because they were allowed to hold the lead on their own. Together, of course. That was the rule.

The park was bustling. Children were playing in the snow, a man was selling hot chestnuts, and on the hill young people were sledging. Suddenly a big grey dog ran past them, off the lead. Fritz barked, jumped, and the lead slipped out of Kuba's hand.
Kuba! You were supposed to hold on tight!
I did hold on tight! But it was so fast!

Fritz ran after the grey dog, over the hill, between the sledges, and then he was gone. The twins searched for half an hour. They shouted “Fritz! Fritz!” until they lost their voices. Then they ran home crying, because they didn't know what else to do.

Ludwig opened the door. He saw the children's red eyes and the empty lead in Ola's hand. For a moment he said nothing. Mara, who was just coming home from work, saw that his face had gone completely white.
We're so sorry, Mr Brandt! It's my fault, because I didn't hold the lead tight!
No, no. It's not your fault. Fritz is a dachshund. Dachshunds are hunters. He saw the dog and thought it was an adventure.
But Mara saw that his hand was shaking. She knew Fritz was more than a dog to Ludwig. Since Ingrid's death, Fritz had been his family, his alarm clock, his reason to get up every morning.
Ludwig, we'll find him. I'm sure we'll find him. The whole building is helping.

Within twenty minutes, Kastanienallee was full of people searching. Lena closed the bakery, even though Saturday was her best day. Piotr took the car and drove slowly through the streets. Kasia printed fifty posters with Fritz's photo: “MISSING! Dachshund Fritz, 8 years old, very friendly, loves sausages.” The twins stuck them on every lamp post.

Even Mrs Hoffmann helped. She couldn't go down the stairs, but she sat at her window on the fourth floor with an old pair of opera glasses and watched the street. Every half hour she rang Lena: “Nothing. Just pigeons.”

Mara and Ludwig went to the Mauerpark together. Ludwig didn't want to wait at home, even though the doctor had said he mustn't go out alone on the ice. “I'm not alone,” he said. “You're here, after all.”

It got dark. It got colder. They asked every person in the park. A boy had seen a small brown dog, “maybe an hour ago, towards the Gleimtunnel”. A woman thought she had seen him on Bernauer Straße. But there was nothing on Bernauer Straße.
At eight o'clock they were sitting on a cold bench in the park. Ludwig hadn't said anything for hours. Then he said, very quietly:

You know, Mara, Ingrid chose Fritz. He was the smallest puppy and nobody wanted him, because he was so skinny. Ingrid said: “We'll take this one. Because otherwise nobody will take him.” A year later she was ill. I think she knew I would need someone.
Mara took his good hand. At that moment her phone rang. It was Lena. She was almost shouting.
Come home! Right now! He's here! He's sitting in front of the bakery!

When they arrived ten minutes later, Fritz was sitting on the step in front of the bakery, dirty, wet and very pleased with himself. Next to him lay an enormous bone, which certainly didn't come from Prenzlauer Berg. The twins were sitting to his left and right, holding him tight with both hands in his fur.
Where did he get this bone?

Nobody ever found out. Nobody knows even today. Ludwig knelt down on the cold step, cast and all, without thinking about his back, and Fritz licked his face. Ludwig was laughing and crying at the same time.
You old rascal. You silly, wonderful rascal. Do you know the whole building was looking for you?

Fritz didn't know. But he did know that there were sausages for everyone that evening, in Ludwig's flat, under the yellow lamp. And that Kuba secretly slipped him three pieces under the table. Because Kuba thought Fritz was a hero today. And because Kuba was very, very happy.
